articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced the issuance of amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update provides crucial clarifications for financial institutions and individuals navigating U.S. sanctions compliance.

The amendments aim to enhance understanding and streamline the reporting process for apparent violations and blocked property. These FAQs serve as an important resource for ensuring adherence to OFAC regulations and mitigating sanctions risks across various programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. This action reflects ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy in response to evolving geopolitical landscapes.

In conjunction with these changes, OFAC also issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions. These licenses aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, providing specific carve-outs for humanitarian aid or other permitted activities.
The designations and removals underscore the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions programs, which are continuously evaluated and updated to address national security and foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations are part of a broader effort to combat intellectual property theft and protect American innovation.

Accompanying these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses are intended to provide guidance and authorization for certain transactions that may be impacted by the new PAIPA designations, ensuring that legitimate activities can continue while targeting illicit conduct.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This amendment provides updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela.
The changes reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. policy concerning Venezuela, aiming to refine the scope of authorized activities under the sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation. These actions target entities and individuals deemed to be involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions. These measures aim to provide clarity and specific authorizations for certain transactions, while maintaining pressure on the designated entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a specific adjustment to the sanctions program targeting Venezuela.

Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in the designated party's behavior, a shift in U.S. foreign policy, or a determination that the designation no longer serves its intended purpose.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations under its counter narcotics and counter terrorism sanctions programs. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and supporting terrorist activities globally.
These designations aim to disrupt the financial networks of criminal organizations and terrorist groups, thereby limiting their ability to operate and threaten international security.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today issued a new Russia-related General License. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the existing Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are frequently used to allow for specific types of humanitarian, administrative, or other transactions that are deemed not to undermine the overall objectives of the sanctions regime.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 Over Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., for $11,662,930. The settlement resolves apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This penalty is part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC. Bank of America admitted to processing millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs.
OFAC determined that Bank of America's apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, with no reduction to the base penalty for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics for $175,015. This settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
Details of the specific violations were not immediately released, but such settlements typically involve breaches of sanctions programs related to designated countries, entities, or individuals.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $1,427,230 against an individual for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This action underscores OFAC's enforcement against individuals as well as corporate entities.

While the specific details of the individual's violations were not disclosed, OFAC frequently pursues penalties against individuals who engage in unauthorized transactions with sanctioned countries, entities, or persons, or who facilitate such transactions.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has paid a civil penalty of $60,764 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This settlement highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for all companies, regardless of size or industry.
The enforcement action serves as a reminder that even seemingly minor transactions can lead to significant penalties if they involve sanctioned parties or jurisdictions.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has paid a civil penalty of $1,050,000 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This substantial penalty underscores the critical need for comprehensive sanctions compliance, particularly for firms operating internationally.

The enforcement action against FTI Consulting, a global business advisory firm, emphasizes that companies providing professional services are not exempt from OFAC's stringent requirements and must ensure their activities do not inadvertently support sanctioned entities or regimes.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC

This significant fine highlights OFAC's aggressive enforcement posture against major international corporations.

The substantial penalty against Adani Enterprises, a prominent Indian multinational conglomerate, signals a strong message regarding the severe consequences of non-compliance with U.S. sanctions, particularly for entities with extensive global operations. The specific nature of the violations leading to this record-setting penalty was not immediately detailed.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 to OFAC

This enforcement action underscores the importance of robust compliance programs for financial services firms, particularly those involved in international transactions.

The penalty against TradeStation Securities, an online brokerage firm, serves as a reminder that firms must diligently screen clients and transactions to prevent engagement with sanctioned individuals, entities, or jurisdictions, and to ensure adherence to all applicable U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3,777,000 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations

The enforcement action demonstrates that individuals who engage in or facilitate transactions with sanctioned parties or jurisdictions face significant financial repercussions. The specific nature of the violations leading to this penalty was not immediately disclosed.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
